listing_view.reasoning: Subscription went from ~2.9x to 88.4x on the final day, which signals a strong demand surge at a price (13.7x latest basic EPS vs a stated 18.31x benchmark) the seller appears to have priced to clear. Nothing in the data shows whether that demand is sticky institutional money or listing-flip momentum, so a debut pop is plausible but the quality of the book is unverifiable.

longterm_view.reasoning: Reported profits grew ~22% CAGR, but the latest year's profit did not arrive as cash (operating cash flow of -121 against EBITDA of 648), and ROCE has fallen every year from 47.5% to 28.8% while debt climbed to ~2294. A business compounding accounting earnings while consuming cash and returning less on each rupee of capital is not one I'd pay 13-14x for without better evidence the cash conversion recovers.

governance.reasoning: Related-party unsecured loans from promoters, director-guaranteed bank facilities, and a show cause notice from the Department of Commercial Taxes are yellow flags individually [promoters, page 325][promoters, page 358][litigation, page 445]. On top of that, our own recomputation of debt-to-equity (1.18) disagrees with the document's printed 0.23, which means at least one statement in the filing does not reconcile.

key_risks.risk: Cash conversion broke down in the latest year
key_risks.why_it_matters: Operating cash flow swung from +341.6 to -121.0 while PAT hit a record, so the reported earnings quality depends on future collections/liquidation of working capital.

key_risks.risk: Declining returns on capital with rising leverage
key_risks.why_it_matters: ROCE fell from 47.5% to 28.8% while total debt roughly doubled, meaning growth is being bought with capital at falling efficiency.
The ₹12,047m order book underpins the growth story, but the document itself warns that future business procurement is becoming more uncertain and that cost/time overruns hurt financials.
Promoters extend unsecured loans and personal guarantees to the company, so minority shareholders bear related-party and key-person financing risk.

answers.question: where did the money go — receivables, inventory, or both?
answers.answer: Not receivables: receivable days collapsed from 94 to 19.5 over two years, so customers are paying much faster even as cash flow turned negative. By elimination, the working-capital drain is most likely inventory and/or contract work-in-progress, but no inventory figure was provided, so I cannot prove it — the negative operating cash flow alongside faster collections is only consistent with a non-receivable working-capital build (or a payables unwind).

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: A disclosed working-capital schedule showing the negative cash flow is a one-off inventory build already converting back to cash, plus resolution of the 1.18 vs 0.23 debt-to-equity discrepancy, would materially lift the long-term view. Conversely, confirmation that the gap is unbilled contract revenue would push it lower.
